query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superior corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily due to the in situ selective oxidation of chromium, which enriches at the alloy surface to form a dense, adherent Cr‐rich passive oxide layer that retards further corrosive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline steels with controlled alloying compositions, including variations in Cr (and possibly Mo) content typical of nuclear and chemical-processing steels (e.g., conventional 304 stainless steel as a baseline composition).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Cr content in otherwise compositionally similar steels and expose them to simulated service environments using a controlled in situ electrochemical cell combined with operando spectroscopic monitoring (e.g., XPS or Raman spectroscopy).
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated primary water or acidic/chloride-containing environments at high temperature (~320 °C) and high pressure (approximately 11 MPa), with parameters adjusted to mimic realistic nuclear or chemical-processing conditions. Optionally, irradiation conditions may also be included to address nuclear service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a protective, Cr-enriched oxide scale (e.g., Cr2O3 or related spinel structures) that acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: Under aggressive environmental conditions, preferential dissolution of Fe occurs relative to Cr. The liberated Cr is then rapidly oxidized, resulting in the selective enrichment of a Cr-rich passive film at the metal surface, which limits further corrosion by acting as an effective barrier.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with higher Cr content will exhibit an earlier and more rapid formation of a dense and adherent Cr-rich passive oxide layer. Measurements will show higher Cr enrichment on the oxide surface, lower corrosion current densities, and elevated pitting potentials compared to steels with lower Cr levels (baseline).
generation.baseline: Conventional 304 stainless steel or similar steels with lower, non-optimized Cr content for passivation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under the defined simulated aggressive environments (high-temperature water, acidic or chloride additives, and controlled pressure) that closely mimic chemical-processing and nuclear power conditions; it might not apply outside these specific environmental parameters or on steels with significantly different microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of Cr is strongly implicated, the contributions of other minor alloying elements (e.g., Mo) and microstructural factors (e.g., grain size, precipitate formation) may also affect passivation. The transient kinetics of oxidation and the exact quantitative impact under varying conditions remain to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of steel samples that are identical except for systematically varied Cr content. Expose these samples in a high-pressure, high-temperature autoclave containing an aggressive solution (e.g., 0.5 M H2SO4 or chloride-containing solutions) that replicates service environments. Use in situ surface analysis (such as operando XPS or Raman spectroscopy) combined with electrochemical measurements (e.g., monitoring corrosion current densities and pitting potentials) to track the evolution of the passive oxide film in real time.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and Cr enrichment levels (via operando XPS or similar spectroscopy)
Electrochemical parameters such as corrosion current density and pitting potential
Morphological assessment of the oxide layer (using electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with higher Cr content do not demonstrate statistically significant earlier or enhanced formation of a Cr-rich passive film (i.e., similar oxide composition and corrosion performance to the baseline sample), then the hypothesis that selective Cr oxidation is the governing cause of the observed corrosion resistance would be falsified.

In this study, two kinds of alloys, Al0.05(CrFeNi)0.95 and Al0.25(CrFeNi)0.75, were prepared by arc melting. After processing, the alloys were exposed to 320 °C, 11.3 MPa, high-temperature water containing HBO3 and LiOH for 20, 40, and 60 days, respectively. The weight change, phase structure, microscopic morphology, and composition of the oxidation product were analyzed in detail, and the following conclusions were obtained. Al0.05(CrFeNi)0.95 is a FCC single-phase HEA (denoted as F0), and the oxidation product on the surface after corrosion is mainly (FeCrNi)3O4. The dense (FeCrNi)3O4 spinel particles formed a corrosion barrier, which greatly improved the corrosion resistance of the F0 alloy. Al0.25(CrFeNi)0.75 is a BCC single-phase HEA (referred to as B0), and the oxidation products on the surface after corrosion are mainly Ni1.94O3H0.81 and Al2O3. Al2O3 will generate easily soluble AlOOH in high-temperature water, which will seriously damage the integrity of the oxide film and cause it to fall off. frame.system: Steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, typically with alloying elements that form passive oxide scales (e.g., chromium, molybdenum) in their as-fabricated and service-exposed states.
frame.goal: To explain and validate a mechanistic basis for the enhanced corrosion resistance observed in these steels and establish causality between alloying element behavior (e.g., selective oxidation/passivation) and corrosion performance.
frame.limitation: The exact mechanistic pathway by which alloy chemistry and resulting oxide scale characteristics impart superior corrosion resistance remains uncertain and challenging to isolate under realistic service conditions.

frame.regime: Simulated service conditions relevant to chemical-processing and nuclear power environments, such as exposure to corrosive chemical agents (e.g., chloride-containing solutions or acidic media), high-temperature water environments, and, where applicable, ionizing radiation conditions. Temperature, pressure, and environmental chemistry should mimic those of real-world operation.
prior_attempts: Prior studies have characterized the surface oxide composition and morphology post-exposure; however, they often relied on ex situ analyses that failed to capture transient phenomena during active corrosion.

Empirical correlations between alloy composition and corrosion rates were observed, yet these studies did not implement well-controlled mechanistic experiments to directly link specific alloying behavior (e.g., chromium enrichment dynamics) to corrosion resistance.

decision.trend: Early studies in corrosion for advanced alloys under nuclear and chemically aggressive conditions focused on carefully characterizing the surface scales formed after service exposure. For example, PMC9318428 examined the formation of selective oxide scales (e.g., (FeCrNi)3O4) on HEAs under simulated primary water conditions, linking phase-dependent oxidation to corrosion rates. Later, work such as PMC9955357 employed controlled tests under molten salt conditions, revealing micro‐galvanic effects between different phases and the role of protective enrichment (of noble elements) in passivation. Overall, there has been a steady evolution from ex situ compositional and morphological assessments to more in situ measurements (e.g., Volta potential mapping) that begin to isolate the influence of alloying chemistry on transient oxidation processes.
decision.unsolved: The missing link is a controlled, mechanistic demonstration that explains how selective oxidation of specific alloying elements (e.g., chromium or molybdenum) actively generates a protective, passivating oxide scale during exposure to realistic service environments. The transient evolution, stability, and composition of the oxide layer under operating temperature, pressure, and chemical aggressors (including chlorides, acids, and radiation) remain unprobed, leaving causality as opposed to correlation unestablished.
decision.lever: Implement an in situ electrochemical/spectroscopic study where steels with systematically varied levels of critical alloying elements (e.g., controlled adjustments in Cr and Mo content) are exposed to simulated service environments (e.g., high-temperature water with chloride/acidic additives and, where applicable, irradiation). Key parameters (potential, temperature, concentration) would be varied while real‐time techniques (such as operando XPS, Raman spectroscopy, or synchrotron-based methods) monitor the onset and evolution of selective oxidation and scale formation relative to a baseline of conventional composition.
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the progression from ex situ characterization to dynamic, real‐time measurement, allowing the experimenters to test the hypothesis that selective oxidation/passivation of key alloying elements is the governing cause of corrosion resistance. It is precisely tuned to reveal causality under realistic conditions and offers a clear falsification pathway: if no transient enrichment or protective oxide formation is observed despite controlled variation of elemental content and environmental conditions, the hypothesis would be invalidated.

families.principle: Using advanced, real-time characterization techniques to capture transient, dynamic processes such as the formation, evolution, and repair of the passive oxide scales under simulated service conditions.

challenge of observing the mechanism under realistic conditions

families.best_lever: Implement in situ spectroscopy (e.g., in situ XPS or Raman) or advanced electron microscopy (e.g., environmental TEM) to monitor the rapid formation and repair of passive oxide layers during exposure to simulated corrosive agents.

families.principle: Integrating controlled experiments with advanced in situ characterization and atomistic/mesoscale simulations to offer a comprehensive, cross-validated understanding of the corrosion resistance mechanism.
cues_for: the need to connect mechanistic predictions with empirical observations
limitations of prior studies that only provided ex situ data
the multifaceted challenge of testing hypotheses under realistic, corrosive conditions

families.best_lever: Couple in situ characterization (e.g., real-time XPS or E-TEM during corrosion tests) with atomistic simulations to dynamically track the formation and evolution of passive oxide scales, allowing direct comparison with predictions and enabling targeted falsification of the hypothesis.

families.principle: Isolating individual variables under controlled laboratory conditions to directly link alloy composition and environmental factors to corrosion behavior, relying on empirical observation and reproducible alterations in service conditions.
